title: Transfer: 3Sum, Every Triplet That Sums to Zero
oneLiner: Find every distinct triplet that adds up to 0. Sort once, fix the first number, and the rest is the sorted Two Sum scan you already know.
keyTakeaway: A k-sum problem on sorted input peels down to two pointers: fix nums[i], then find pairs summing to -nums[i] in the part to its right with left and right moving inward. Skipping equal neighbours, both for the fixed number and after each match, is what keeps the triplets distinct.
explanation:
This follows Two Sum on a Sorted Array, with the requirement changed twice: three numbers instead of two, and every answer instead of one. Given an unsorted array nums, return every distinct triplet [a, b, c] of values at three different positions with a + b + c = 0. Write each triplet in ascending order and list the triplets in ascending order (compare the first value, then the second), with no triplet repeated.

Trying every triple is O(n^3). Sort first (O(n log n), and it also makes duplicate handling easy). Then for each index i, the question "which two numbers to the right of i sum to -nums[i]?" is exactly the sorted Two Sum problem on nums[i + 1 ..]: left = i + 1, right = n - 1, move left up when the sum is too small and right down when it is too big. The only change inside the scan is that a match does not end it: record the triplet, move both pointers inward, and keep going, because other pairs may also work.

Duplicates are the part that needs care. If nums[i] equals nums[i - 1], every triplet it could start was already found, so skip it. After a match, step left past every copy of the value just used (and right likewise), or [-2, 0, 0, 2, 2] reports [-2, 0, 2] twice. Because the array is sorted and i, left and right only move forward and inward, the triplets come out already in the required order.

A small speed-up: once nums[i] is greater than 0, everything to its right is too, so no triplet can sum to 0 and the outer loop can stop. Overall O(n^2): n choices of i, each with an O(n) scan.

The visualization runs the sorted array [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]; the highlighted cells are i, left and right.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences on why the two pointer scan is still correct inside each fixed i. Why does moving left up (or right down) never skip a valid pair, and what exactly does sorting buy you twice in this problem?

visualizationSteps.message: Sorted: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. Fix each i in turn and look for a pair to its right summing to -nums[i].
i = 1: -1 + -1 + 2 = 0. Record [-1, -1, 2], then move both pointers inward past repeats and keep scanning.
i = 1: -1 + 0 + 1 = 0. Record [-1, 0, 1], then move both pointers inward past repeats and keep scanning.
i = 2: nums[2] = -1 equals the previous value, so every triplet it starts was already found. Skip it.
Done: [-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]. Each fixed i ran the sorted Two Sum scan once, so the whole thing is O(n^2).

recognitionSignals: Find all distinct combinations of a fixed small size (three, four) that hit a target sum.
You are allowed to sort, and the answer is about values, not original indices.
gotchas: Skip a fixed value equal to the previous one, and skip repeats after each match, or the same triplet appears more than once.
Don't stop the scan at the first match: other pairs to the right of i can also work.
A hash set of triplets removes duplicates too, but costs extra memory and still needs sorted triplets to compare.
confusableWith: Hash Maps: Two Sum keeps a map because its input is unsorted and it must return original indices. Here sorting is allowed, so two pointers need no map.

complexity.note: Sorting is O(n log n); then each of n fixed values runs one O(n) two pointer scan, so O(n²) dominates. Space is the sorted copy (O(1) extra if you sort in place, ignoring the sort's own stack and the output).
